Q: Unsigned 128-bit division on 64-bit machine A:

For cases where you can't rely on __int128 being available, check out the cppalliance/int128 library that was released in 2025.

Boost.Int128 is a portable implementation of a signed, and an unsigned 128-bit integer and related functionality (e.g. bit counting). Importantly, on all platforms, the sizeof the types provided in this library are 128-bits.

The library is header-only, has no dependencies, and requires only C++14.

Q: Accessing metadata/ attributes of a netcdf file in terra A:

The coordinates attributes tells you that the data variable "t" (in CF-speak, this is what terra turns into a SpatRaster) is 8-dimensional. Before you try to visualize that in your mind, there are only 4 "true" axes (in the sense that the actual array of the data variable is 4D) "lon", "lat", "time" and "member", with the 5th axis "height2m" being a scalar coordinate variable (more CF-speak). The 3 remaining "dimensions" are in fact labels attached to the member axis. These labels are netCDF variables like all the other "dimensions" but GDAL apparently does not read them and terra can thus not see them.

Otherwise you are out-of-luck because reading the netCDF file (the one I have over here with 34 members) with terra produces a SpatRaster as a 3D array, merging the member and time axes into one. Why that is I do not know, because terra also supports 4D data sets as a SpatRasterDataset. This could be due to way that GDAL reads the netCDF file.

With ncdfCF you can access the data by "gcm_model". The example below extracts a year of data but you could just as easily extract all data for a single GCM model or for some geographic subset, also in combination.

library(ncdfCF)

# Open the netCDF file, see what is inside
fn <- "~/path_to/t_CMIP6_ssp245_mon_201501-210012.nc"
ds <- open_ncdf(fn)
names(ds)
#> [1] "t"

# Grab variable "t" and, as an example, extract the data for this year
t <- ds[["t"]]
tdata <- t$subset(time = c("2025-01-01", "2026-01-01"))

# Grab the "member" axis and list names of the sets of coordinates
m <- tdata$axes[["member"]]
m$coordinate_names
#> [1] "member" "member_id" "gcm_institution" "gcm_model" "gcm_variant"

# Make the desired set of coordinates active
m$active_coordinates <- "gcm_model"

# Now you can create a SpatRasterDataset, which will have proper names set...
library(terra)
#> terra 1.8.29
(r <- tdata$terra())
#> class       : SpatRasterDataset 
#> subdatasets : 34 
#> dimensions  : 180, 360 (nrow, ncol)
#> nlyr        : 12, 12, 12, 12, 12, 12, 12, 12, 12 
#> resolution  : 1, 1  (x, y)
#> extent      : -180, 180, -90, 90  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : +proj=longlat +ellps=WGS84 +no_defs 
#> source(s)   : memory 
#> names       : ACCESS-CM2, ACCESS-ESM1-5, AWI-CM-1-1-MR, BCC-CSM2-MR, CAMS-CSM1-0, CESM2-WACCM, ...

# ... as wekll as on the SpatRasters it contains
r["EC-Earth3-Veg"]
#> class       : SpatRaster 
#> dimensions  : 180, 360, 12  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#> resolution  : 1, 1  (x, y)
#> extent      : -180, 180, -90, 90  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : +proj=longlat +ellps=WGS84 +no_defs 
#> source(s)   : memory
#> names       : 2025-01-01, 2025-02-01, 2025-03-01, 2025-04-01, 2025-05-01, 2025-06-01, ... 
#> min values  :  -43.19824,  -40.50879,  -47.00879,  -51.64355,  -58.46680,  -52.64648, ... 
#> max values  :   38.09766,   37.27539,   35.53711,   35.34082,   37.71777,   39.25391, ...

# So you can refer to the names in plotting and other processing
plot(r["EC-Earth3-Veg"]["2025-05-01"])

Q: API calls to api.weather.com - Daylight savings date format A:

This is a classic DST gap problem. On March 8, 2026 (US Spring Forward), clocks jumped from 2:00 AM to 3:00 AM EST→EDT, so that calendar day is only 23 hours long in local time.

The API almost certainly anchors its day boundaries to local midnight, meaning:

  • March 7 ends at 2026-03-08 00:00:00 EST

  • March 8 starts at 2026-03-08 00:00:00 EST = 2026-03-08 05:00:00 UTC

  • March 8 ends at 2026-03-09 00:00:00 EDT = 2026-03-09 04:00:00 UTC

When you request startDate=20260307 it likely interprets that as UTC midnight, which lands you in the middle of the local March 7, causing it to either skip or misalign the day boundary entirely.

What to Try

The API probably supports a datetime format even if undocumented. The most common patterns Weather Company APIs accept are:

# ISO 8601 with explicit UTC offset
startDate=20260308T000000-0500    ← local midnight EST explicitly stated

# Or with a separate timezone parameter (worth trying)
startDate=20260308&timezone=America/New_York

# Or Unix timestamp (most unambiguous — highly recommended)
startDate=1741410000              ← 2026-03-08 00:00:00 EST in epoch seconds

Unix timestamps are your most reliable option because they have no ambiguity around DST at all. For KALB (Albany, NY):

DayLocal MidnightUTC EquivalentUnix TimestampMarch 7 start2026-03-07 00:00 EST05:00 UTC1741323600March 8 start2026-03-08 00:00 EST05:00 UTC1741410000March 9 start2026-03-09 00:00 EDT04:00 UTC1741492800

So your request would be:

https://api.weather.com/v1/location/KALB:9:US/observations/historical.json
  ?apiKey=<MY_API_KEY>
  &units=e
  &startDate=1741410000
  &endDate=1741492800

For the Fall-Back Day (November 1, 2026)

The opposite problem occurs — clocks fall back at 2:00 AM EDT→EST, making that day 25 hours long. The hour from 1:00–2:00 AM repeats, and a naive date-only request may drop the repeated hour or duplicate it. Unix timestamps handle this correctly since epoch time is always UTC-based and continuous.

Practical Fix for Your Collection Script

Rather than using startDate with calendar dates, compute Unix timestamps for local midnight of the target station's timezone for every request — not just DST days. This makes DST days consistent with every other day and removes the twice-yearly failure entirely.

python

from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
from datetime import datetime

tz = ZoneInfo("America/New_York")  # KALB timezone

# Local midnight, DST-aware
start = datetime(2026, 3, 8, 0, 0, 0, tzinfo=tz)
end   = datetime(2026, 3, 9, 0, 0, 0, tzinfo=tz)

print(int(start.timestamp()))  # 1741410000
print(int(end.timestamp()))    # 1741492800

Q: Xslt 1.0 check if something exists or empty value? A:

The XPath 1.0 specification states that:

• a string is true if and only if its length is non-zero

Therefore the expression:

boolean(string)

returns false when string is empty, true otherwise.

Conversely, the expression:

not(string)

returns true when string is empty, false otherwise.

Note that there is no need to convert the string explicitly to a boolean when used within the test attribute of xsl:if or xsl:choose. You can do simply:

<xsl:if test="string">
   <!-- do something when string is not empty -->
</xsl:if>

But keep in mind that the above applies strictly to objects of type string. A node such as an element or an attribute evaluates to true by merely existing, even if it's empty. In order for the test to return true only when an attribute exists and is not empty we would do:

<xsl:if test="string(@attribute)">
   <!-- do something -->
</xsl:if>

Q: What is wrong with my PIL looped image paste? A:

There are two bugs here working against you.

Bug 1 — buf.seek(0) is in the wrong place

You're seeking to the start of the buffer before writing to it, which does nothing useful. After plt.savefig(buf) the buffer's read position is at the end, so when PIL tries to open it, it reads nothing. Move the seek to after the save:

python

plt.savefig(buf)
buf.seek(0)  # ← must be here, not before savefig
sw = Image.open(buf)

Bug 2 — y_offset increments by the full composite image height instead of one swatch height

python

y_offset += height   # ← wrong, this is the TOTAL image height

After the first swatch this jumps y_offset way past the bottom of your canvas, so all subsequent pastes land out of bounds and are silently ignored. Change it to:

python

y_offset += sw_height  # ← one swatch height

Bug 3 (latent) — matplotlib figure isn't cleared between iterations

sns.palplot() creates a new figure but previous state can bleed through in some environments. Add a plt.close() at the end of each loop iteration:

python

    sw = Image.open(buf)
    swatches.paste(sw, (0, y_offset))
    y_offset += sw_height
    plt.close()  # ← clean up figure for next iteration

Corrected loop

python

for theme_file in theme_list:
    with open('themes/' + theme_file) as th:
        theme = json.load(th)

    theme_name = theme.pop('name')
    theme_description = theme.pop('description')

    sns.palplot(theme.values())
    plt.title(theme_name)

    for i, key in enumerate(theme):
        plt.text(
            i, 0.2,
            key + '\n' + theme[key],
            ha='center',
            va='bottom',
            color=invert_hex(theme[key]),
            fontsize=7
        )

    plt.tight_layout()
    buf = BytesIO()
    plt.savefig(buf)   # write first
    buf.seek(0)        # then rewind

    sw = Image.open(buf).copy()  # .copy() lets you close the buffer safely
    swatches.paste(sw, (0, y_offset))
    y_offset += sw_height
    plt.close()

swatches.save('theme_swatches.png')
